In the previous lesson, you looked at the internal operation of the 8051 microcontroller. This included registers, the ALU and the control unit.
INTRODUCTIONM

To utilize the functions of these and other internal operations, connections are provided to connect the microcontroller to external circuitry. It is this external circuitry that gives the microcontroller its ability to be useful.
There are many different types of circuits that can be interfaced to a microcontroller. Some circuits are necessary for the controller's operation, like power, memory and the address decoders.
Other connections may not be necessary, based on the application of the microcontroller.
However, not having components like a clock would prevent the microcontroller from operating at all.
In this lesson we will be looking at the necessary external circuitry for the operation of the microcontroller.
The external circuitry that we will look at is the reset circuit and memory. In the next lesson we will look at the parallel port, serial port, keyboard, and display.

In this lesson we are going to discuss the necessary external circuitry required for the microcontroller to operate. Specifically, we will be discussing the reset circuit and external memory connections.
DISCUSSION

The RESET circuitry consists of a normally open switch, two resistors, a diode and a capacitor. These are connected to the RST input signal of the 8051. The name of this pin indicates that if a HIGH condition is applied to this pin, the system will be reset.

We are going to look at the RST input under two conditions: initial power application and when the reset button is cycled. When power is applied to the system, C8 has no charge and presents a very low resistance to the applied voltage and essentially acts like a short...e sh, the capacitor has no charge and acts like a short.

This means that both the top and bottom of the capacitor are at 5 volts which is a HIGH to the 8051 chip. This indicates the system is in a reset condition. Five time constants are required for the capacitor to effectively charge to + 5 volts.

When the capacitor fully charges, the top of the capacitor will be at + 5 volts and the bottom of the capacitor (and pin 9 of the 8051) will be at 0 volts. This represents the non-reset condition of the 8051...ipin will be at 5 volts and the bottom pin will be at 0 volts or a LOW condition. This indicates a non-reset condition.
The 8051 chip construction technology is known to produce a change in HIGH/LOW conditions between 0.8 volts and 2.0 volts.
Somewhere between 2.0 and 0.8 volts, the 8051 will accept the input signal as a LOW condition. This tells the microcontroller that it can start. n. This tells the microcontroller that it can start.

The object of the delay is to ensure all components have had time to reset before the microcontroller starts. To achieve this, the first recognized value of 2.0 volts is used. designed to be long enough to make sure all other components have had time to reset, the delay will have been designed using the lowest possible recognized low value or

This way if the change occurs later, at 1.5 volts for example, it will wait longer than required which is OK. If too short of a delay had been selected, then other components might not have time to reset before the microcontroller starts.. e delay had been designed using a lower voltage and a chip was used with a higher voltage where the transition occurred, the delay would be shorter and all other devices may not be reset yet.

After the system has been operating and you want to reset it, you perform this operation by pressing the reset button. While the reset button is pressed down, the positive end of the charged capacitor is connected to the negative end of the capacitor through a resistor.

This applies + 5 volts to the RST line and initiates the RESET condition. The purpose of diode D1 is to rapidly discharge C8 when power is removed. This ensures that the microcontroller will enter the reset condition upon a brief interruption of power...Since there are no components between the RST and 5 volts, the RESET condition is recognized by the system. The diode provides protection and voltage limitation.
After the button is released, the capacitor begins charging as it did when power was turned on.

Now that we have looked at the reset circuitry, let's look at memory.
There are many chips and signals required for the proper connection of memory to the microcontroller. The graphic below shows the connections of the memory to the 8051 microcontroller.
ADDRESS LATCH
PHPHPHPH

The address and data lines which come out of the microcontroller must be demultiplexed. Address/Data lines AD0 through AD7 are the signals which must be separated into the data and address information. A8 through A15 are just address lines.
In the operation of an instruction which uses memory, the microcontroller has to have a method for multiplexing the address and data information.
This is acheived by making the address information available at beginning of the operation, and making the data available for the remainder of the operation.
Remember, however, that we do need the address information available for the rest of the operation. This is made possible by the use of an address latch.
An address latch will save the high address bits for the remainder of the operation. The address latch outputs are the last input values when the C signal was asserted HIGH.
ADDRESS LATCH

The 8051 ALE signal (Address Latch Enable) is high while the address is on the multiplexed lines, and low while the data is on the lines. The ALE signal is attached to the C input of the address latch.
Again, while the C input is high, the input to the latch is present at the output. When the C input is low, the last input while the C signal was high is present at the output.
This makes all information available at one time. It is important to note that the latches are not bi-directional. Address information is only generated by the microcontroller.
If other devices need to indicate addresses to the microcontroller, they will pass it through the data lines just like any other data.
Now that you know how the address information is made available, let's look at how the memory chips are attached and controlled by the microcontroller.
There are two types of memory that can be attached to the 8051 microcontroller: ROM and RAM. The first type is EPROM memory, or Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory.
ADDRESS LATCH

This memory is programmed by a special device and cannot be changed without the use of other special devices. It contains the monitor program which is used when the system is first turned on or is reset.. the system is first turned on.

The EPROM is made up of one chip, U3, which is a 27C256 chip. This IC is 32 kbytes of read only memory. Since a byte is 8 bits, the chip holds 256 kbits of data. This is where the 256 in the chip's name comes from.' , which derives the 256 in the IC name.

Next to the EPROM is the location for the second type of memory, the RAM chip. The main difference between ROM and RAM is RAM can be written to as well as read. However, unlike ROM, the information is lost power is removed. This location contains 32 kbytes of RAM, known as the 62256 chip............location contains 32 kbytes of RAM, known as the 62256 chip.
We need to look at the signals which are used to control the memory chips. Address lines A0 through A14 are connected directly to the A0 through A14 connections of both memory chips.
Each chip contains 32 thousand memory locations. The microcontroller can address 64 thousand locations with just the address lines, and 128 thousand using a combination of other signals.
For this reason, the last available address line is used to pick between the two chips. This method of using the additional address line is known as chip select decoding.
The address line used to select between the EPROM and the RAM is A15. We also need to introduce a few other signals which also affect whether or not a memory chip is selected.

The PSEN (Program Store Enable) signal from the microcontroller is used to select between reading program memory or writing data and accessing IO. If the signal is low, then the microcontroller is trying to read information from external memory.
If this signal is high, then the microcontroller is trying to write information to RAM or access an IO device.

The last two control signals from the microcontroller to memory are the RD and WR. These are the read and write signals. If the WR line is low, then the microcontroller is trying to write information to memory.
ADDRESS LATCH
When the RD line is low then the microcontroller is trying to read information from memory. When both lines are high, the microcontroller is neither reading or writing.
Both lines cannot be low at the same time because the microcontroller cannot read and write simultaneously.
Now that you have been introduced to the signals generated by the microprocessor, let's see how they are connected to the external circuitry.

Address line 15 connects directly to the CS or chip select line of the EPROM chip. Address line 15 is also applied to both inputs of a NAND gate. In this configuration the NAND gate works like an inverter.

The inverted A15 signal is then connected to the chip select pin CS of the RAM. Since the CS pins turn on the chip when the applied signal is low, the EPROM will be on when A15 is low and the RAM will be on when A15 is high.

The chip select signals do not place information on the data bus, they just allow the other control signals to be active on the memory chips. The other control signals are output enable and write enable.
The PSEN and RD signals are connected to the inputs of a NAND gate, inverted through another NAND gate and applied to the OE or output enable of the RAM chip.

For the output of the RAM to occur, either PSEN or RD have to be low. This occurs when the microcontroller reads external memory. The PSEN signal is connected directly to the OE or output enable of the EPROM.

Since you can only read from an EPROM, this is the only signal you need. It is important to note that you could connect the RD line to the EPROM, but in this situation it would just be redundant information.
Lastly, the WR signal from the microcontroller is connected to the WE or write enable pin of the RAM chip. When writing from the microcontroller, the PSEN signal is always high.

For this reason the WR or write line is able to be directly connected to the WE of the RAM without other signals. When designing circuitry, it is important to make sure that only the specific chip and function of that chip is used at a specific time.

It is important to note how memory is connected in any particular 8051 system will depend on the size and number of memory chips used. However, the manner in which they are connected will be relatively the same. er of memory chips used. However, the way in which they are connected will be relatively the same.

From the graphic below and the knowledge of the program you entered, you can easily see the operations being performed by the microcontroller.
A15 is always HIGH indicating that we are reading/writing to RAM. Remember that A15 is inverted and attached to the CS (chip select) pin of the RAM chip. Notice also that the RD line never goes low.
You may be wondering how it is reading information from RAM. Remember that external instructions are read with the PSEN signal. We are only reading instructions and their information.
If we were trying to read data from RAM and not instructions, the RD signal would go low and not the PSEN signal.
The first two low pulses of the ALE and PSEN signal load 74 into the instruction register and 0A into a temporary register. The next pulse performs the action which moves 0A into the accumulator (A).
The next three pulses of these signals load the next instruction and its immediate data. Note that this data is considered part of the instruction which is why the RD line is not active (low).

The next pulse is the instruction being performed which moves the16-bit value 8100 into the DPTR register. The next pulse loads the instruction F0 which is MOV @ DPTR,A. This will take the value stored in A and put it into the memory pointed to by DPTR.

Since we are writing data to external memory, the PSEN signal is not needed. You can see that the WR signal goes low and the ALE signal goes low. This indicates the writing of information to RAM. Notice how much longer this instruction takes.

Internal memory transfers are much faster. After this, the last instruction and data is read which is three bytes long. This accounts for the three low pulses of PSEN and ALE which load the instruction and information.
The last low pulse loads the value 8000 into the program counter (PC) and returns to the beginning of this program. This is the periodic program that you entered into the system.

Two additional observations need to be discussed regarding the ALE and PSEN signal. ALE is address latch enable which means when it is high the address on the address/data bus needs to be latched by the latches. This is why the PSEN signal does not go low until after the ALE signal has gone low.
This makes sure that the address information is valid. Second is the extra low pulse of PSEN and ALE when the microprocessor is performing the action. This has to do with the design of the system.

Each read from external memory actually causes two PSEN low pulses and two ALE low pulses. When the system is reading many memory locations sequentially, the last pulse of the previous read and the new pulse of the next read overlap.
This is why there is an extra set at the end where no new read is needed. This is where the microcontroller is actually performing operations internally.

From the graphic below and the knowledge of the program you entered, you can easily see the operations being performed by the microcontroller.
A15 is always HIGH indicating that we are reading/writing to RAM. Remember that A15 is inverted and attached to the CS (chip select) pin of the RAM chip. Notice also that the RD line never goes low.
You may be wondering how it is reading information from RAM. Remember that external instructions are read with the PSEN signal. We are only reading instructions and their information.
If we were trying to read data from RAM and not instructions, the RD signal would go low and not the PSEN signal.
The first two low pulses of the ALE and PSEN signal load 74 into the instruction register and 0A into a temporary register. The next pulse performs the action which moves 0A into the accumulator (A).
The next three pulses of these signals load the next instruction and its immediate data. Note that this data is considered part of the instruction which is why the RD line is not active (low).

The next pulse is the instruction being performed which moves the16-bit value 8100 into the DPTR register. The next pulse loads the instruction F0 which is MOV @ DPTR,A. This will take the value stored in A and put it into the memory pointed to by DPTR.

Since we are writing data to external memory, the PSEN signal is not needed. You can see that the WR signal goes low and the ALE signal goes low. This indicates the writing of information to RAM. Notice how much longer this instruction takes.

Internal memory transfers are much faster. After this, the last instruction and data is read which is three bytes long. This accounts for the three low pulses of PSEN and ALE which load the instruction and information.
The last low pulse loads the value 8000 into the program counter (PC) and returns to the beginning of this program. This is the periodic program that you entered into the system.

Two additional observations need to be discussed regarding the ALE and PSEN signal. ALE is address latch enable which means when it is high the address on the address/data bus needs to be latched by the latches. This is why the PSEN signal does not go low until after the ALE signal has gone low.
This makes sure that the address information is valid. Second is the extra low pulse of PSEN and ALE when the microprocessor is performing the action. This has to do with the design of the system.

Each read from external memory actually causes two PSEN low pulses and two ALE low pulses. When the system is reading many memory locations sequentially, the last pulse of the previous read and the new pulse of the next read overlap.
This is why there is an extra set at the end where no new read is needed. This is where the microcontroller is actually performing operations internally.
